title: A route to damage tolerance exceeding $10\%$ in shuttling-equipped quantum processors
abstract: This is a short study of an approach offering high tolerance to damage (i.e. defects or 'drop outs') in solid state fault-tolerant quantum computing. Our method is primarily aimed at semiconductor electron spin-qubit systems, which have been shown to support fast and high-fidelity shuttling along pre-defined paths. We adapt the recent CAbLECAR method of Chadwick and Chong: stabilisers are performed by ancillas which each follow a bespoke pre-programmed path. We consider the simple surface code but we damage the physical lattice, and rely on route-solving software to find efficient pathways under constraints enforcing stabiliser commutation and hook error avoidance. Solutions are then converted to detector error models for Stim and logical error rates are obtained. We express our results by gauging the logical performance against that of a pristine lattice, using the notion of a reduced equivalent surface-code distance; for reasonable underlying error rates we find that $10\%$ damage leaves roughly half of the pristine equivalent distance ($d_\text{equiv}\approx0.48\,d_\text{pristine}$ in the large-array limit, rising to $\approx0.60$ for our smallest array). This suggests that one can tolerate substantial damage by building oversized arrays. We note that investigating damage tolerance of other qLDPC codes is a straightforward generalisation, and potentially one could adapt to damage emerging at runtime.
summary: This work proposes an advanced method to maintain fault tolerance in shuttling quantum processors despite significant physical damage. By adapting pathfinding algorithms to route syndrome measurements around defective lattice sites, the authors show that 10% damage only reduces the effective code distance by a predictable factor. This demonstrates that mobility significantly enhances hardware robustness compared to fixed-qubit approaches.
main_problem: The study addresses how fault-tolerant quantum computation can maintain functionality when subjected to physical damage (defects or 'drop outs') in the underlying hardware.
main_result: The proposed shuttling-based method allows for substantial damage tolerance, achieving performance equivalent to a pristine lattice with only 48% to 60% of its distance even after 10% node deletion.
method: It adapts the CAbLECAR method by using route-solving software on time-expanded graphs to find efficient paths for ancillas performing syndrome measurements around damaged physical lattices.
model_or_system: The model is based on semiconductor electron spin-qubit systems configured in a latticework architecture supporting shuttling. It implements the surface code and simulates damage by deleting nodes from this lattice structure.
key_observables: Logical error rate (LER), reduced equivalent surface-code distance ($d_{	ext{equiv}}$), and the maximum achievable code distance ($d$).
important_parameters: Damage fraction ($f$), shuttle error rate ($p_{	ext{shuttle}}$), idling error rate, and the lattice size ($G 	imes G$ array).
main_assumptions: The damage is assumed to be static and known before runtime; the analysis focuses on the surface code in memory mode.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the latticework structure showing pristine vs. 10% deleted nodes, detailing location, path, and ancillary node placements.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of damage tolerance in shuttling qubits, details the adaptation of CAbLECAR using route-solving on damaged lattices, presents results quantifying performance degradation via $d_{	ext{equiv}}$, and concludes by generalizing the approach to other QLDPC codes.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, quantitative framework for assessing hardware resilience in solid-state quantum computing platforms, directly addressing scalability limitations imposed by physical defects.

Filled blue circles are location nodes occupied by a data qubit; white circles are unoccupied locations. Green and red squares are emitter and receiver nodes, where ancillas are injected and read out; small grey circles are path nodes forming the shuttle corridors. Deleted nodes, and nodes pruned because deletion disconnected them from the main component, are shown as light crosses. FIG. 2. The distance-d rotated surface code (shown for d = 5): d2 data qubits, with d2 −1 X (red) and Z (blue) stabilisers in a checkerboard, and weight-two boundary sta- bilisers as lobes. The hook-error-avoiding N–Z syndrome- extraction ordering [27, 28] is shown for each stabilizer: X- type ancillas visit their corner data qubits in the “Z”-shaped order NW→NE→SW→SE, Z-type ancillas in the “N”-shaped order NW→SW→NE→SE. The four steps form one global schedule; boundary stabilisers simply skip their missing cor- ners.

FIG. 3. Mean equivalent distance ¯dequiv at 10% deletion (6 × 6 grid, X basis) as a function of the dephasing shuttle error rate. Each point maps the damaged samples’ best LER onto an equivalent pristine distance via the same-noise pris- tine fit; error bars are the standard error of the mean (SEM). The curve is nearly flat below ∼2 × 10−4 and falls steeply above it, where the pristine log-linear fit also begins to break down (R2 dropping from 0.99 to 0.86) as the code approaches threshold. Asterisks mark the operating points where this equivalent-distance mapping is becoming unreliable — a de- graded pristine fit (R2 < 0.95) and/or some samples whose LER falls beyond the pristine reference...

FIG. 4. Idling sensitivity at 10% deletion (6 × 6 grid), with the shuttle rate fixed at 2 × 10−4. Top: mean equivalent dis- tance ¯dequiv vs the idling target pidle (error bars are the SEM). Bottom: the composition of the winning code size d∗across samples, with ¯d∗overlaid. The shaded band marks the tip- ping region (1 × 10−3–2 × 10−3) where the winning distance departs its low-noise d = 9 plateau and the equivalent dis- tance tips down. Asterisks (top panel) mark points where the equivalent-distance mapping is becoming unreliable — a de- graded pristine fit (R2 < 0.95) and/or extrapolated samples — as the code nears threshold, exactly as in Fig. 3.

Fig. 4 fixes the shuttle rate at this primary value and sweeps the idling target. Below ∼10−3 the winning code size sits on a stable d = 9 plateau; between 10−3 and 2 × 10−3 the winning distance collapses off that plateau and the equivalent distance tips downward in lockstep. We adopt pidle = 10−3 as our baseline — the low edge of this tipping region, i.e. the largest idling error still short of the collapse. As established in the error model, this baseline is already about 20 times more pessimistic than the ∼5×10−5 implied by demonstrated silicon T2 times, so it is a conservative operating point in absolute terms as well.
